steps.body: Two more exponent rules translate. Division subtracts exponents, so **log_b (M/N) = log_b M − log_b N**. And a power multiplies its exponent, so **log_b (Mᵖ) = p · log_b M** — the exponent inside marches out front. Check: log₂ (8²) = log₂ 64 = 6 = 2 · 3. ✓

widget.prompt: Evaluate log₃ 81 − log₃ 3 as a single log: log₃ (81/3) = log₃ 27 = ?

commonErrors.feedback: The subtraction DIVIDES the insides: 81/3 = 27, and log₃ 27 = 3 (4 is log₃ 81 alone).
27 is the quotient inside — its log (the exponent) is 3.

steps.body: The power property is the workhorse of the whole subject: it drags an unknown **down from the exponent**. log₂ (x⁵) = 5 log₂ x — and later, taking log of both sides of 2^x = 10 will pull the x down where algebra can reach it. Special case: roots. log₉ (√9) = log₉ (9^(1/2)) = **1/2**.

explanationVariants: log₂ (x⁷) = 7 log₂ x — the exponent becomes a coefficient.
Powers inside multiply the log outside.

commonBuilds.feedback: The exponent moves OUT as a multiplier — it doesn't raise the whole log to a power.
x⁷ is a POWER, not the product 7 · x — the 7 exits as a coefficient.
The base never changes — only a coefficient 7 appears: 7 log₂ x.

widget.missFeedback: The power property drops the exponent 7 to a COEFFICIENT in front: 7 log₂ x.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the power property moves the 7 out front.

widget.prompt: Rewrite log₅ (√x) using the power property.

options.label: (1/2) log₅ x
options.feedback: Right — √x = x^(1/2), and the 1/2 marches out front.

options.label: log₅ x − log₅ 2
options.feedback: That's the QUOTIENT rule on x/2 — a square root is the POWER 1/2.

options.label: 2 log₅ x
options.feedback: The root HALVES the exponent (1/2 out front); 2 would square it.

options.label: √(log₅ x)
options.feedback: The power exits as a coefficient — it never wraps the log itself.

explanationVariants: log₃ (x/9) = log₃ x − log₃ 9 = log₃ x − 2.
Split the quotient; the numeric piece evaluates.

commonBuilds.feedback: DIVISION subtracts: the 9 underneath leaves with a MINUS sign.
The bottom exits as a subtracted log (worth 2) — it never divides the log.
Order matters: the NUMERATOR's log comes first — log₃ x − 2.

widget.missFeedback: The quotient splits with a MINUS, numerator first: log₃ x − log₃ 9, and log₃ 9 = 2.
widget.successFeedback: Right — the quotient splits, and log₃ 9 = 2.

explanationVariants: Power out, then evaluate the small log.

numericErrors.feedback: The power MULTIPLIES the log (5 · 2), it doesn't add to it (5 + 2).

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

explanationVariants: log₂ (8x³/y) = log₂ 8 + log₂ x³ − log₂ y = 3 + 3 log₂ x − log₂ y.
Product splits to +, quotient to −, the power exits: three rules, one line.

commonBuilds.feedback: y sits UNDERNEATH — the quotient rule sends it out with a minus.
Logs add and subtract when insides multiply and divide — they never multiply each other.
log₂ 8 = 3 stands ALONE as an added constant — the x³'s coefficient 3 belongs only to log₂ x.

widget.missFeedback: Product→add, power→coefficient, quotient→subtract: log₂8=3, then +3 log₂ x, then −log₂ y.
widget.successFeedback: Right — product, power, and quotient properties in sequence.

hints: Split the product: log₂ 8 + log₂ (x³) − log₂ y.
log₂ 8 = 3; the power property turns log₂(x³) into 3 log₂ x.

steps.body: Quotients subtract; powers march out front.
takeaways: log_b(Mᵖ) = p log_b M — the equation-solving superpower.
Roots ride the same rule with fractional powers.
steps.teaser: Next: fluency drills — expanding and condensing multi-part expressions.

concept.body: The power rule in pure numbers: log₂ (2³) asks '2 to what power gives 2³?' — the exponent is sitting right there.

explanationVariants: The property just formalizes reading the exponent.

commonErrors.feedback: 2³ = 8 is the INSIDE — the log returns the exponent: 3.
